title: Agents
summary: What an agent really is (a model, some tools and a loop), how MCP lets tools plug into any agent, and how to tell when a plain workflow is the better build.
youWillLearn: That an agent is a model calling tools in a loop until it decides it is done
How to write that loop, and which limits it always needs
What MCP is, and why it matters for apps you sell
How to decide between an agent and a simple workflow

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.tool use: You describe functions to the model, and it can reply with a request to call one. Your code runs it and sends back the result.
glossary.agent: A program where a model decides its own next step, calls tools, reads the results, and repeats until the task is done.
glossary.agent loop: The code that keeps calling the model, running the tools it asks for, and sending back the results, until it stops asking.
glossary.workflow: A fixed sequence of steps written in code, where the model fills in specific steps but does not choose what happens next.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for plugging tools and data into AI apps, so one tool server works with many different agents.
glossary.MCP server: A small program that offers tools (and sometimes data) over MCP, such as "search notes" or "create issue".
glossary.side effect: A change in the outside world caused by a tool, such as sending an email, deleting a row or charging a card.

steps.title: Notely's chat can look things up
body: Maya, a Notely user, chats with our notes app. The app server (the computer running Notely's code) passes her question to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI.
Thanks to tool use (lesson 4), Claude can ask the server to search her notes in the database (where notes live), then answer. One question: two model calls, three seconds.

scene.caption: Claude asks for a search, the app server runs it, Claude answers.

steps.title: "Plan my week from my notes"
body: Maya asks: "Plan my week from my notes and my calendar." Her calendar is a separate service, outside Notely. Claude must read recent notes, check the calendar, maybe search for a deadline it just spotted, then write the plan.
You cannot list those steps in advance. What to look up second depends on what it found first.
changes: + Calendar: Maya's calendar, a service outside Notely
~ Claude API: does not know which step comes next

scene.caption: Two places to look, and no fixed order to look in.

steps.title: An agent is a model in a loop
body: An agent is tool use, repeated. Claude asks for a tool; your code runs it and sends back the result. Claude asks for another, or decides it has enough and answers.
The model chooses each next step. Your agent loop keeps going until it stops asking. More steps means more calls and a longer wait.

callout.text: A detective with a phone. Each call's answer decides who they ring next. You cannot script the calls in advance, but you can decide whose numbers they have.

changes: ~ App Server: runs the loop, tool after tool
~ Model calls 2 → 5
~ Wait time 3 → 15 s

scene.caption: Ask, run, return, repeat: the model picks each next tool.

steps.title: The loop, in about a dozen lines
body: Call the model with the tools. Add its reply to the history. If stop_reason is not tool_use, you are done. Otherwise run the tools, add the results, and go again.
Note the step limit. A loop without one can run, and bill, for a very long time. SDKs also ship a tool runner that writes this loop for you.

code.caption: runTools runs each tool request as this user and returns the matching results.

changes: ~ App Server: the loop gets a limit of 10 steps

scene.caption: The loop lives in your code, and your code sets its limit.

steps.title: Tools are the agent's hands
body: An agent is only as good as its tools. Give it a few clear ones, not thirty, and return errors it can act on: "No notes match 'logo'. Try a broader query."
Split tools that read from tools with side effects. Reading the calendar is harmless. Creating or deleting events is not, and deserves Maya's yes.

callout.text: Tool results go back into the model's context. Return what it needs, like titles and short excerpts, not whole tables. Big results make every later step slower and pricier.

changes: ~ Calendar: reading is free, changing it needs Maya's yes
~ Database: returns short excerpts, not whole notes

scene.caption: Read tools run freely; tools that change things wait for a person.

steps.title: MCP: one plug for every agent
body: MCP is an open standard: an MCP server offers tools once, and any app that speaks MCP can use them.

You already use this: Supabase or GitHub servers in Claude Code. Notely could ship one, so Maya searches her notes from Anthropic's Claude app. It checks who is asking, so each user sees only their notes.

code.code:
# connect Claude Code to a remote MCP server
claude mcp add --transport http notely https://notely.app/mcp
code.caption: Same server, many apps. A real one needs sign-in, so it acts only as that user. The URL is made up.

changes: − Maya, App Server, Claude API, Calendar
+ Notely MCP: offers Notely's tools to any AI app
+ Claude Code, Claude App, Your Agent: three AI apps using it
~ Database: each user still sees only their notes

scene.caption: One Notely MCP server, plugged into three different AI apps.

steps.title: Most features do not need an agent
body: Agents are slower, cost more, and are less predictable, because the model chooses the path. Use the simplest thing that works.

One model call: summaries. A workflow, where your code fixes the steps (fetch, call the model, save): a weekly plan. An agent only when the steps truly cannot be known ahead, like open-ended research.

callout.text: Clients often ask for "an agent" when they mean "an AI feature". Propose the simplest version that meets the goal. It is cheaper to run, easier to test, and quicker to ship.

changes: − Claude Code, Claude App, Your Agent, Notely MCP, Database
+ Summary, Weekly Plan, Research: simplest to most open

scene.caption: Pick the simplest build that does the job.

steps.title: Notely's planner: workflow first
body: Look again at "plan my week". It almost always needs the same two things: last week's notes and next week's calendar. So code fetches both at once and makes one model call.
Faster, cheaper, and testable with fixed inputs. If users later need open-ended digging, the planner can grow into an agent.

code.caption: Your code picks the steps. The model does the part only it can do: the planning.

changes: − Summary, Weekly Plan, Research
+ Maya, App Server, Claude API, Database, Calendar: back
~ Model calls 5 → 1
~ Wait time 15 → 6 s

scene.caption: Code fetches notes and calendar, then makes a single call to plan.

steps.title: Loops that never stop
body: When you do build an agent, expect it to get stuck sometimes: calling the same tool again and again, each call re-sending a growing history.
Cap the steps and total tokens. Ask before any side effect. Log every step to replay it later. Tool results are untrusted text too: a note can try to steer the agent (lesson 9).

callout.text: When Claude Code builds an agent, ask: what is the max number of steps? Is there a token or time budget? Which tools change data, and do they need approval? Is every tool call logged? Could a workflow do the job?

changes: ~ App Server: an agent loop again, stuck searching
~ Database: searched nine times for the same thing
~ Model calls 1 → 10
~ Wait time 6 → 60 s

scene.caption: The same search, over and over, each call costing more than the last.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: An agent is a model choosing tools in a loop. Your code runs the tools, caps the steps, asks before side effects, and logs everything. MCP lets one tool server work with many AI apps.
Most features are better as one call or a workflow. Reach for an agent only when the steps cannot be known in advance.
changes: ~ App Server: back to the planner workflow
~ Database and Calendar: one fetch each
~ Model calls 10 → 1
~ Wait time 60 → 6 s

scene.caption: Simple, capped, predictable: the right amount of AI.

quiz.question: What makes something an agent rather than a workflow?

options.text: It uses more than one model call.
options.why: A workflow can make several calls too. The difference is who decides the steps.

options.text: The model decides the next step based on what it found, in a loop.
options.why: In a workflow your code fixes the sequence. In an agent the model picks each next tool call until it decides it is done.
MCP is a way to plug in tools. Workflows and agents can both use it, or not.

quiz.question: A salon owner, Sam, wants "an AI agent" that texts each client a reminder the day before their booking. What do you propose?

options.text: An agent with tools to read bookings and send texts, running every hour.
options.why: The steps are fully known. An agent adds cost, delay and a way to send wrong texts, for no gain.

options.text: A model call that decides whether reminders are needed at all.
options.why: Whether to remind is a fixed business rule. Code can decide it reliably.

options.text: A scheduled job: code selects tomorrow's bookings and sends a text, maybe with a model writing a friendly message.
options.why: Fixed steps belong in code. The model, if used at all, fills in one step: the wording.

quiz.question: Claude Code built an agent loop with while (true) and a delete_note tool that runs without asking. What do you ask for first?

options.text: A step limit and budget, and a user confirmation before delete_note runs.
options.why: Loops can get stuck and keep billing, and tools with side effects need a human yes. Both limits belong in code.

options.text: A better system prompt telling it to never loop and to be careful with deletes.
options.why: Prompts help, but they are not limits. The code must enforce the cap and the approval.

options.text: A larger model, so it makes fewer mistakes.
options.why: Even the best model can loop or misread a request. Limits are needed regardless of model size.

takeaways: An agent = model + tools + a loop. The model picks the next step; your code runs it.
Every agent loop needs a step limit, a budget, approval before side effects, and a log of every step.
Give agents a few clear tools with useful errors and small results.
MCP lets one tool server plug into Claude Code, Claude apps and your own agents.
Start with one call, then a workflow. Build an agent only when the steps cannot be known in advance.
